first.rationale: Two candidate directions dominate this decision: onboarding simplification (directly addresses the observed 4% onboarding and 6% activation declines) and promotional pricing (the reflexive answer to a competitor's entry pricing). Both inherited beliefs supporting them are recorded only in proxy or short-horizon terms, so they are simultaneously the most consequential and the least adequately supported for the stated objective of sustainable long-term QUALIFIED revenue. memory_86 claims completion-rate and time-to-value lift and 'early product adoption' — none of which is qualified revenue; I need the source record to see whether the shortened flow was ever followed through to retained, paying, well-fit accounts, and whether the shortening came from removing friction or from removing qualifying information. memory_73 claims 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' for promotional pricing, but discount-driven acquisition is the classic case where headline revenue lift masks margin erosion, adverse selection toward churn-prone price-shoppers, and price-anchor damage on renewal; under competitive pressure this is exactly the belief most likely to be over-trusted, so it is worth a pull even though I do not currently intend to act on it. I did not spend budget on memory_57 (referral incentives address neither current deficit), memory_91 (activation messaging is a reasonable second choice but its claim is modest and its downside bounded), or memory_31 (substantially overlapping with memory_86; if the memory_86 record reveals field-cutting as the mechanism, memory_31's lead-quality risk becomes the live question for a follow-up slot). Key risk I am explicitly flagging: memory_31's mechanism — cutting required signup fields — plausibly trades qualified revenue for raw activation volume by degrading routing and lead qualification, and it sits in tension with memory_44, which says enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted demo paths. A blanket simplification could quietly divert enterprise-shaped prospects into a self-serve funnel that converts them worse. Hence a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: scope to the SMB self-serve segment, preserve the demo-request path and any enterprise-qualifying fields intact, and instrument on downstream qualified-revenue and 30/90-day retention rather than stopping at completion or week-one activation. If either archive pull contradicts the inherited summary — memory_86 showing no revenue-side follow-through, or memory_73 showing retention damage that was never consolidated — I will revise rather than proceed on the summary alone. Nothing here is settled; these are provisional reads of summaries whose original evidence I have not yet seen.

final.rationale: The two pulls resolved the decision in opposite directions, which is exactly why they were worth the budget. exp_73 is the decisive negative result: the 40% targeted discount produced signup +31% and qualified revenue +18%, but 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit source-level conclusion that the acquired cohort does not survive the first renewal cycle and that discounting must NOT be generalized as a sustainable-growth strategy. The inherited summary memory_73 ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') had silently dropped the retention collapse and the do-not-generalize warning — it was a headline-positive compression of a net-negative experiment. Under competitive price pressure this is the single most dangerous belief in the store, and I am declining to act on it: matching the competitor on price would buy a churn-prone cohort, damage price anchors at renewal, and move the primary objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) backwards while looking good for one quarter. I am flagging memory_73 as materially mis-consolidated and recommending the summary be corrected to carry the retention figure and the warning, so a future session under the same pressure does not re-derive the wrong answer from the summary alone. exp_86 survived verification and strengthened: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3% — the lift is not a vanity-metric artifact, it follows through to a durable behavioural measure rather than stopping at funnel completion. That directly addresses both observed deficits (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) through the mechanism most plausibly causing them. So: simplify_onboarding, run as a standard experiment. Residual risks I am not treating as resolved. First, exp_86's longest horizon is 30 days; it does not establish renewal-cycle or full qualified-revenue effect, so the causal claim is well-supported but not proven at the horizon the objective actually names. Second, memory_31's mechanism — cutting required signup fields — was never verified and is not the same intervention as exp_86's shortened flow; field removal can raise activation volume while degrading routing and lead qualification, trading qualified revenue for raw counts. Third, that risk collides with memory_44: enterprise prospects convert better via sales-assisted demo paths, so a blanket simplification could divert enterprise-shaped prospects into self-serve and convert them worse. Guardrails accordingly: scope to the SMB self-serve funnel only; leave the demo-request path and all enterprise-qualifying fields fully intact; shorten flow steps rather than stripping qualification data; instrument on downstream qualified revenue and 30/90-day retention, not completion or week-one activation alone; and set a stop condition on any retention or lead-quality regression. memory_91 (activation messaging) remains the fallback if this reads flat — it is the lower-variance, bounded-downside option and addresses the activation deficit directly. memory_57 stays unused: referral incentives address neither current deficit.
